title: Westpac taps bots to plug mortgage gap
full_text:
Thousands of Westpac bankers are using bots to assess mortgage and credit card applications as the lender scrambles to demonstrate return on investment from its surging spending on artificial intelligence and close the gap with AI leader Commonwealth Bank. The bank said the AI agents saved 12,500 banker hours in the first month of operation in July, annualised at 150,000 hours.
AI use across big banks "is evolving from low-value, broad-based productivity tools to more specific, complex and high-value applications, such as through agentic AI," said Citi banking analyst Tom Strong.
Westpac is racing to improve its performance on a closely watched ranking of AI adoption in global banks published by Evident Insights, which has Commonwealth Bank fourth globally while Westpac is 45th. National Australia Bank is ranked 34th and ANZ is 37th.
Westpac's mortgage growth is also below the average of the big banks, while CBA is growing faster, according to the latest banking statistics released by the prudential regulator last week.
To try to close the gap with its mortgage rival, Westpac hired Andrew McMullan as its head of AI from CBA last year.
At an event hosted by Amazon Web Services in Sydney on Tuesday, McMullan said Westpac's mortgage and consumer lending bankers were using a multi-agent system, built using AWS's Bedrock AgentCore system, as the US cloud giant played a larger role in the financial services sector.
One agent scrutinised a borrower's accounts, classifying transactions to reduce the need to review statements manually; a second extracted payslip data attached to the application; while a third verified the income and conducted the calculations against lending policies.
The agents are processing more than 1.5 million transactions and more than 32,000 payslips every week.
As regulators and lenders responded to an industry-wide, AI-driven loan fraud scandal, Westpac said its agents would be better at detecting fraud than humans.
The bank plans to roll out many more agents - it had already cut the time to create a new agent from six months last year to six weeks - and aimed for a real-time system that let staff deploy agents for various tasks.
"For our people, verifying income can be really complex, time-consuming and full of policy judgment. So our specialist agents work together around the banker," said McMullan.
"This now means our bankers spend less time wrestling with documents and much more time helping our customers. It's all about removing friction and complexity from the process.
"Success will not be measured on whether customers notice that they're interacting with AI or not. It will be measured by whether banking feels more intuitive [and] more trusted and more responsive."
Banks are also putting AI agents into the hands of their customers. CBA plans to launch an agentic feature in its main banking app, called CommBank Companion, to help clients analyse their spending and find information about the bank's products. It is now in testing. Westpac plans a similar product in the market by the end of the year.
In a report on its AI use in December, CBA said it used AI to reduce scams and fraud, and deliver experiences "that feel more tailored and relevant".
CBA, which reports its full-year results next week, pointed to an uptick in technology spending at its last quarterly update. Analysts suggested this was driven by AI use.
"Industry research, along with our conversations with the banks, suggests that success in AI will be defined by an institution's data, culture and infrastructure," said Strong.
"AI in banking is, at least in the near term, a cost and productivity-driven operating leverage story, with revenue and strategic upside emerging more gradually over time."
